narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 52% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. Placing in the second decile is noticeably lower than the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among students who were admitted. This low ranking signaled to the model a higher risk that you might struggle with the bar exam.

Your LSAT score of 35.5 worked in the opposite direction, pulling the prediction toward passing. Although the score is only modestly below the 37.2 average of accepted students, the model still viewed it as a meaningful positive signal. Unfortunately, this helpful influence was not large enough to overcome the negative effect of your third-year class rank.

Your first-year class rank came in third in importance and also pushed toward failure. Ranking in the bottom decile after your first year, compared with an average around the sixth decile for accepted students, reinforced the model’s concern about long-term academic performance.

Taken together, these academic signals created just enough doubt for the model to forecast a slightly higher than 50% chance of failing the bar. To strengthen future applications, focus on raising your class standing in the remaining years and consider retaking the LSAT to boost that score. These improvements would directly address the factors that most influenced this decision. (248 words)
